Homarus gammarus , known as the European lobster or common lobster , is a species of clawed lobster from the eastern Atlantic Ocean , Mediterranean Sea and parts of the Black Sea . It is closely related to the American lobster , H. americanus . It may grow to a length of 60 cm ( 24 in ) and a mass of 6 kilograms ( 13 lb ) , and bears a conspicuous pair of claws . In life , the lobsters are blue , only becoming " lobster red " on cooking . Mating occurs in the summer , producing eggs which are carried by the females for up to a year before hatching into planktonic larvae . Homarus gammarus is a highly esteemed food , and is widely caught using lobster pots , mostly around the British Isles . 
 Homarus gammarus is a large crustacean , with a body length up to 60 centimetres ( 24 in ) and weighing up to 5 – 6 kilograms ( 11 – 13 lb ) , although the lobsters caught in lobster pots are usually 23 – 38 cm ( 9 – 15 in ) long and weigh 0 @.@ 7 – 2 @.@ 2 kg ( 1 @.@ 5 – 4 @.@ 9 lb ) . Like other crustaceans , lobsters have a hard exoskeleton which they must shed in order to grow , in a process called ecdysis ( moulting ) . This may occur several times a year for young lobsters , but decreases to once every 1 – 2 years for larger animals . 
 The first pair of pereiopods is armed with a large , asymmetrical pair of claws . The larger one is the " crusher " , and has rounded nodules used for crushing prey ; the other is the " cutter " , which has sharp inner edges , and is used for holding or tearing the prey . Usually , the left claw is the crusher , and the right is the cutter . 
 The exoskeleton is generally blue above , with spots that coalesce , and yellow below . The red colour associated with lobsters only appears after cooking . This occurs because , in life , the red pigment astaxanthin is bound to a protein complex , but the complex is broken up by the heat of cooking , releasing the red pigment . 
 The closest relative of H. gammarus is the American lobster , Homarus americanus . The two species are very similar , and can be crossed artificially , although hybrids are unlikely to occur in the wild since their ranges do not overlap .  Female H. gammarus reach sexual maturity when they have grown to a carapace length of 80 – 85 millimetres ( 3 @.@ 1 – 3 @.@ 3 in ) , whereas males mature at a slightly smaller size . Mating typically occurs in summer between a recently moulted female , whose shell is therefore soft , and a hard @-@ shelled male . The female carries the eggs for up to 12 months , depending on the temperature , attached to her pleopods . Females carrying eggs are said to be " berried " and can be found throughout the year . 
 The eggs hatch at night , and the larvae swim to the water surface where they drift with the ocean currents , preying on zooplankton . This stage involves three moults and lasts for 15 – 35 days . After the third moult , the juvenile takes on a form closer to the adult , and adopts a benthic lifestyle . The juveniles are rarely seen in the wild , and are poorly known , although they are known to be capable of digging extensive burrows . It is estimated that only 1 larva in every 20 @,@ 000 survives to the benthic phase . When they reach a carapace length of 15 mm ( 0 @.@ 59 in ) , the juveniles leave their burrows and start their adult lives .

It is also present in most of the Mediterranean Sea , only missing from the section east of Crete , and along only the north @-@ west coast of the Black Sea .  The species can be divided into four genetically distinct populations , one widespread population , and three which have diverged due to small effective population sizes , possibly due to adaptation to the local environment . The first of these is the population of lobsters from northern Norway , which have been referred to as the " midnight @-@ sun lobster " . The populations in the Mediterranean Sea are distinct from those in the Atlantic Ocean . The last distinct population is found in the Netherlands : samples from the <unk> were distinct from those collected in the North Sea or English Channel . 
 Attempts have been made to introduce H. gammarus to New Zealand , alongside other European species such as the edible crab , Cancer pagurus . Between 1904 and 1914 , one million lobster larvae were released from hatcheries in Dunedin , but the species did not become established there . 
 Adult H. gammarus live on the continental shelf at depths of 0 – 150 metres ( 0 – 492 ft ) , although not normally deeper than 50 m ( 160 ft ) . They prefer hard substrates , such as rocks or hard mud , and live in holes or crevices , emerging at night to feed .

 Air Vice Marshal Frank Headlam , CB , CBE ( 15 July 1914 – 23 December 1976 ) was a senior commander in the Royal Australian Air Force ( RAAF ) . Born and educated in Tasmania , he joined the RAAF as an air cadet in January 1934 . He specialised in flying instruction and navigation before the outbreak of World War II . In April 1941 , he became commanding officer of No. 2 Squadron , which operated Lockheed Hudsons . The squadron was deployed to Dutch Timor in December , and saw action against Japanese forces in the South West Pacific . After returning to Australia in February 1942 , Headlam held staff appointments and training commands , finishing the war a group captain . 
 Headlam served as Officer Commanding North @-@ Western Area in 1946 , and as Director of Training from 1947 to 1950 . In 1950 – 51 , during the Malayan Emergency , he was stationed at Singapore as commander of No. 90 ( Composite ) Wing and , later , RAF Tengah . He twice served as acting Air Member for Personnel , in 1957 and 1959 – 60 , receiving appointment as a Commander of the Order of the British Empire in 1958 . Promoted air vice marshal , he successively held the positions of Air Officer Commanding ( AOC ) Operational Command in 1961 – 62 , AOC No. 224 Group RAF from 1962 to 1965 during the Indonesia – Malaysia Konfrontasi , Deputy Chief of the Air Staff in 1965 – 66 , and AOC Support Command in 1966 – 67 . He was appointed a Companion of the Order of the Bath in 1965 . Following a posting to London as Head of the Australian Joint Services Staff from 1968 to 1971 , he retired from the Air Force and died in Melbourne five years later . 
 The son of farmers Malcolm and Hilda Headlam , Frank Headlam was born on 15 July 1914 in Launceston , Tasmania . He was schooled at <unk> College , Hobart , and matriculated in 1932 . He underwent flying instruction with No. 1 Flying Training School ( FTS ) at RAAF Point Cook , Victoria , and was commissioned as a pilot officer on 1 January 1935 .

No larger than a flight according to the official history of the pre @-@ war RAAF , Seaplane Squadron was part of No. 1 FTS and operated Supermarine Southampton flying boats and de Havilland Gipsy Moth floatplanes , among other types . During this posting Headlam was promoted to flying officer , on 1 July 1935 , and wrote a paper on national defence in which he suggested that with " strong air forces , naval forces ( including submarines ) , and fixed defences , Australia may be made practically invulnerable " . According to Air Force historian Alan Stephens , this paper " in effect , defined the ' anti @-@ lodgment ' concept which has been a persistent feature of RAAF strategic thinking " . 
 Headlam completed a flying instructors course in July 1936 and joined the staff of No. 1 FTS . He was promoted to flight lieutenant on 1 March 1937 . Commencing in July 1938 , he was one of six students to take part in the RAAF 's first Long Specialist Navigation Course , run by Flight Lieutenants Bill Garing and Alister Murdoch at Point Cook . The course involved several epic training flights that attracted considerable media attention , including a twelve @-@ day , 10 @,@ 800 @-@ kilometre ( 6 @,@ 700 mi ) round @-@ Australia trip by three Avro Ansons , one of which was piloted by Headlam , in November . The following month , Headlam led the three Ansons on a six @-@ day journey back and forth over Central Australia . He subsequently passed the navigation course with a special distinction . On 27 January 1939 he was posted to RAAF Station Laverton , Victoria , as a flight commander . He served initially with No. 2 Squadron , before transferring to No. 1 Squadron on 29 August . Both units operated Ansons . 
 Following the outbreak of World War II , No. 1 Squadron was engaged in convoy escort and maritime reconnaissance duties off south @-@ eastern Australia . Headlam continued to serve with the squadron as a flight commander until 15 January 1940 , when he was assigned to Headquarters Laverton as the station navigation officer . On 27 March he was posted to the staff of RAAF Headquarters , Melbourne . He was promoted to squadron leader on 1 June 1940 . Two weeks later he married Katherine Bridge at St Paul 's Anglican Church in Frankston ; the couple would have a son and a daughter . 
 Headlam was given command of No. 2 Squadron at Laverton on 15 April 1941 , and raised to wing commander on 1 July . Equipped with Lockheed Hudsons , the squadron mainly conducted maritime patrols in southern waters until 5 December , when four of its aircraft were ordered to Darwin , Northern Territory , in response to fears of Japanese aggression in the Pacific . On 7 December , this detachment established itself at Penfui , near Koepang in Dutch Timor , while No. 2 Squadron 's eight remaining Hudsons were stationed at Darwin on standby . The following day , aware that Australia was now at war in the Pacific , one of the Penfui @-@ based Hudsons attacked the Japanese <unk> Nanyo Maru , which was suspected of being a radio ship , and forced it aground . By 12 December , Headlam had transferred to Penfui as commanding officer of the base , as well as No. 2 Squadron .

Eastern Area Command , considered a de facto operational headquarters owing to the preponderance of combat units under its control , was reorganised as Home Command in October 1953 . He was promoted to acting air commodore in May . His appointment as aide @-@ de @-@ camp to Queen Elizabeth II was announced on 7 October 1954 . 
 Headlam was promoted to substantive air commodore on 1 January 1955 . In November he was posted to RAAF Overseas Headquarters , London , and the following year undertook studies at the Imperial Defence College . Returning to Australia , he served as acting Air Member for Personnel at the Department of Air , Canberra , from 19 March to 21 October 1957 , between the terms of Air Vice Marshals Fred Scherger and Allan Walters , and again from 24 August 1959 to 28 March 1960 , between the terms of Walters and Air Vice Marshal Bill Hely . In this role Headlam occupied a seat on the Air Board , the service 's controlling body that comprised its senior officers and was chaired by the Chief of the Air Staff . He was also one of two RAAF representatives to serve on a committee , chaired by businessman William John Allison , examining conditions of defence service ; the committee 's recommendations led to a doubling of flight pay , among other improvements . Headlam 's other positions at the Department of Air included Air Commodore Plans from October 1957 to January 1959 , and Director General Plans and Policy from January to August 1959 . The latter assignment put him in charge of the RAAF 's Directorate of Intelligence . Headlam was appointed a Commander of the Order of the British Empire ( CBE ) in the 1958 Queen 's Birthday Honours , gazetted on 3 June . In May 1960 he became acting Deputy Chief of the Air Staff . 
 On 30 January 1961 , Headlam joined the staff of Operational Command ( OPCOM ) , the successor organisation to Home Command , responsible for the direction of RAAF operational units . He took over as Air Officer Commanding ( AOC ) OPCOM from Air Vice Marshal Val Hancock in April . Headlam was promoted to air vice marshal on 29 May . On 17 July 1962 , he was posted to RAAF Base Butterworth , Malaya , and took up the appointment of AOC No. 224 Group RAF in Singapore one week later . He was succeeded as AOC OPCOM by Air Vice Marshal Alister Murdoch . As AOC No. 224 Group , Headlam had overall responsibility for regional air defence and offensive air operations during the Brunei Rebellion in December 1962 , and the subsequent Konfrontasi between Indonesia and Malaysia that officially began the following month . Divorced from his first wife in 1956 , he married widowed social worker Vernon Spence at the Sydney registry office on 20 January 1964 . He handed over No. 224 Group to Air Vice Marshal Christopher Foxley @-@ Norris on 30 November . 
 Returning to Australia , Headlam became Deputy Chief of the Air Staff ( DCAS ) on 26 January 1965 . He was appointed a Companion of the Order of the Bath ( CB ) " in recognition of distinguished service in the Borneo Territories " on 22 June . His tenure as DCAS coincided with the most significant rearmament program the Air Force had undertaken since World War II , and with manpower shortages stemming from this expansion and from Australia 's increasing involvement in the security of South East Asia . The first RAAF helicopters were committed to the Vietnam War towards the end of his term , and he travelled to Saigon with the Chief of the General Staff , Lieutenant General Sir John Wilton , in March 1966 to plan the deployment . The year before , Wilton had recommended to Air Marshal Murdoch , the Chief of the Air Staff , that two Iroquois be sent to Vietnam for familiarisation purposes ; Murdoch had rebuffed Wilton , and the RAAF helicopter squadron was considered underprepared for its army co @-@ operation role when it finally did deploy . On 1 January 1968 , Headlam was posted to London as Head of the Australian Joint Services Staff . He served as an Extra Gentleman Usher to the Queen from 17 November 1970 to 5 June 1971 . 
 Returning to Australia in June 1971 , Headlam took resettlement leave before retiring from the Air Force on 3 August . He made his home in Melbourne , where he died aged 62 on 23 December 1976 , after a lengthy battle with cancer . Survived by his children and his second wife , he was given a private funeral and cremated at Springvale Crematorium .

 The current M @-@ 82 dates back to 1926 . It ran from US 31 in Hart to the northern junction of US 131 and M @-@ 46 in Howard City . rewritten: Homarus gammarus, commonly referred to as the European or common lobster, is a species of clawed lobster found in the eastern Atlantic Ocean, the Mediterranean Sea, and sections of the Black Sea. It is closely related to the American lobster, known scientifically as H. americanus. This lobster can reach lengths of up to 60 cm (24 in) and weights of up to 6 kilograms (13 lb), and is notable for its prominent claws. In their natural state, these lobsters are blue, turning the iconic "lobster red" only after being cooked. They mate during the summer, with females carrying the eggs for up to a year until they hatch into planktonic larvae. Highly valued as a delicacy, Homarus gammarus is extensively harvested using lobster pots, particularly around the British Isles.

Homarus gammarus is a sizable crustacean, reaching lengths of up to 60 centimeters (24 inches) and weights of 5 to 6 kilograms (11 to 13 pounds), though those typically caught in lobster traps measure between 23 to 38 cm (9 to 15 inches) and weigh from 0.7 to 2.2 kg (1.5 to 4.9 pounds). Similar to other crustaceans, lobsters possess a rigid exoskeleton that they must molt to grow, a process known as ecdysis. Young lobsters may undergo this molting several times annually, whereas older, larger lobsters do so once every one to two years.

The initial set of pereiopods features a significant, uneven pair of claws. The bigger claw, known as the "crusher," is equipped with rounded nodules for smashing prey, while the smaller one, called the "cutter," has sharp inner edges for gripping or shredding the prey. Typically, the crusher is on the left side, and the cutter is on the right.

The exoskeleton typically displays a blue color on top, marked with merging spots, and is yellow underneath. The red hue seen in lobsters emerges only after they are cooked. This change happens because the red pigment astaxanthin, which is attached to a protein complex during the lobster's life, is freed when the heat from cooking breaks down the complex.

The American lobster, Homarus americanus, is the nearest kin to H. gammarus. These two species share many similarities and can be interbred artificially, though natural hybrids are improbable as their habitats do not intersect. Several traits allow for the differentiation between the two species.

Female H. gammarus achieve sexual maturity at a carapace length of 80 – 85 millimeters (3.1 – 3.3 inches), while males reach maturity at a slightly smaller size. Mating usually takes place in the summer between a female who has recently molted and thus has a soft shell, and a male with a hard shell. The female holds the eggs for up to 12 months, depending on the temperature, attached to her pleopods. Females with eggs are referred to as "berried" and can be observed year-round.

The eggs hatch during the night, and the resulting larvae ascend to the surface of the water, where they float with the ocean currents while feeding on zooplankton. This phase includes three moults and extends over a period of 15 to 35 days. Following the third moult, the juvenile begins to resemble the adult more closely and shifts to a benthic mode of living. These juveniles are seldom observed in their natural environment and remain largely mysterious, though it is known that they can create extensive burrows. It is believed that only one out of every 20,000 larvae makes it to the benthic stage. Once the juveniles reach a carapace length of 15 mm (0.59 in), they exit their burrows and commence their adult existence.

Homarus gammarus is distributed throughout the north-eastern Atlantic Ocean, ranging from northern Norway to the Azores and Morocco, but it is absent from the Baltic Sea. It is also found in the majority of the Mediterranean Sea, except for the area east of Crete, and is present only along the north-western coast of the Black Sea. The species' northernmost populations are located in the Norwegian fjords, within the Arctic Circle.

The species is categorized into four genetically unique groups: one extensive group and three others that have diverged because of limited effective population sizes, potentially as a result of adapting to their local environments. The first group consists of lobsters from northern Norway, known as the "midnight sun lobster." The Mediterranean Sea populations are separate from those in the Atlantic Ocean. The final distinct group is located in the Netherlands, where samples from the <unk> differed from those taken in the North Sea or English Channel.

Efforts were made to establish H. gammarus in New Zealand, along with other European species like the edible crab, Cancer pagurus. From 1904 to 1914, a million lobster larvae were released from hatcheries in Dunedin, yet the species failed to establish a population there.

Adult H. gammarus inhabit the continental shelf at depths ranging from 0 to 150 meters (0 to 492 feet), though typically not beyond 50 meters (160 feet). They favor hard surfaces like rocks or firm mud, residing in holes or crevices and coming out at night to forage for food.

Homarus gammarus is vulnerable to the disease <unk>, which is caused by the bacterium <unk> <unk>. While this disease is commonly observed in American lobsters, it has only been detected in captive H. gammarus, particularly in tanks previously used by H. americanus, which could not be excluded as a factor.

Homarus gammarus has long been "highly esteemed" as a culinary delicacy and is referenced in the seventeenth-century English folk song "The <unk>." This species can command very high prices and is available fresh, frozen, canned, or in powdered form. The claws and abdomen of H. gammarus are sources of "excellent" white meat, while most of the cephalothorax is also consumable, except for the gastric mill and the "sand vein" (gut). The price of H. gammarus can be up to three times that of H. americanus, and it is regarded as having a superior flavor.

Lobsters are primarily captured using lobster pots, though occasionally, lines baited with octopus or cuttlefish can lure them into nets or allow them to be caught by hand. In 2008, a total of 4,386 tons of H. gammarus were harvested in Europe and North Africa, with 3,462 tons (79%) of this catch coming from the British Isles, including the Channel Islands. The smallest legal size for landing H. gammarus is a carapace length of 87 mm (3.4 inches).

H. gammarus serves as the type species for the genus Homarus Weber, established in 1795, as officially designated by Direction 51 of the International Commission on Zoological Nomenclature. Before this ruling, there was confusion due to the species being known by various names such as Astacus marinus Fabricius, 1775, and Homarus vulgaris H. Milne-Edwards, 1837. Additionally, the confusion was compounded by the fact that Friedrich Weber's original description of the genus had been overlooked until Mary Rathbun rediscovered it, which invalidated any earlier designations of type species for Homarus H. Milne-Edwards, 1837, in relation to Homarus Weber, 1795.

The lectotype of Homarus gammarus, designated by <unk> Holthuis in 1974, originated from coordinates 57° 53′ N, 11° 32′ E, close to Marstrand, Sweden, which is approximately 48 kilometers or 30 miles northwest of Gothenburg. Unfortunately, both the lectotype and the <unk> have been lost since then.

Air Vice Marshal Frank Headlam, CB, CBE (15 July 1914 – 23 December 1976) served as a high-ranking officer in the Royal Australian Air Force (RAAF). Originally from Tasmania, where he was born and educated, he enlisted in the RAAF as an air cadet in January 1934. Before World War II began, he focused on flying instruction and navigation. In April 1941, he took command of No. 2 Squadron, flying Lockheed Hudsons. The unit was sent to Dutch Timor in December and engaged Japanese forces in the South West Pacific. Upon returning to Australia in February 1942, Headlam took on various staff and training roles, ending the war with the rank of group captain.

In 1946, Headlam was the Officer Commanding North-Western Area, and from 1947 to 1950, he was the Director of Training. During the Malayan Emergency in 1950-51, he was based in Singapore, commanding No. 90 (Composite) Wing and subsequently RAF Tengah. He acted as Air Member for Personnel on two occasions, in 1957 and 1959-60, and was honored as a Commander of the Order of the British Empire in 1958. After being promoted to air vice marshal, he held several key positions: Air Officer Commanding (AOC) Operational Command from 1961-62, AOC No. 224 Group RAF from 1962 to 1965 during the Indonesia-Malaysia Konfrontasi, Deputy Chief of the Air Staff from 1965-66, and AOC Support Command from 1966-67. In 1965, he was made a Companion of the Order of the Bath. After serving as Head of the Australian Joint Services Staff in London from 1968 to 1971, he retired from the Air Force and passed away in Melbourne five years later.

Frank Headlam, born to farmers Malcolm and Hilda Headlam on July 15, 1914, in Launceston, Tasmania, attended <unk> College in Hobart and graduated in 1932. Despite his parents' objections, he enlisted in the Royal Australian Air Force (RAAF) as an air cadet on January 16, 1934. He received his flight training at No. 1 Flying Training School (FTS) at RAAF Point Cook in Victoria and was commissioned as a pilot officer on January 1, 1935.

After finishing a conversion course, Headlam was posted to the Seaplane Squadron at Point Cook. Described as no larger than a flight in the official pre-war RAAF history, the Seaplane Squadron belonged to No. 1 FTS and flew Supermarine Southampton flying boats and de Havilland Gipsy Moth floatplanes, along with other aircraft types. During his time there, Headlam was promoted to flying officer on July 1, 1935, and authored a paper on national defense, proposing that Australia could be made nearly invulnerable with "strong air forces, naval forces (including submarines), and fixed defenses." Air Force historian Alan Stephens noted that this paper effectively established the 'anti-lodgment' concept, which has remained a consistent element in RAAF strategic thought.

Headlam finished his flying instructors course in July 1936 and subsequently joined the team at No. 1 FTS. He received a promotion to flight lieutenant on March 1, 1937. Starting in July 1938, he was among six participants in the RAAF's inaugural Long Specialist Navigation Course, led by Flight Lieutenants Bill Garing and Alister Murdoch at Point Cook. This course featured several notable training flights that drew significant media coverage, such as a twelve-day, 10,800-kilometer (6,700 miles) journey around Australia completed by three Avro Ansons, with Headlam piloting one of them in November. The next month, Headlam commanded the three Ansons on a six-day trip to and from Central Australia. He excelled in the navigation course, earning a special distinction. On January 27, 1939, he was assigned to RAAF Station Laverton in Victoria as a flight commander. Initially, he was with No. 2 Squadron before moving to No. 1 Squadron on August 29. Both squadrons flew Ansons.

After World War II began, No. 1 Squadron took on roles in convoy escort and maritime surveillance along the southeastern coast of Australia. Headlam remained with the squadron as a flight commander until January 15, 1940, after which he was transferred to Headquarters Laverton to serve as the station navigation officer. On March 27, he joined the staff at RAAF Headquarters in Melbourne. He received a promotion to squadron leader on June 1, 1940. Two weeks following his promotion, he wed Katherine Bridge at St Paul's Anglican Church in Frankston; they later had a son and a daughter.

On 15 April 1941, Headlam took command of No. 2 Squadron at Laverton and was promoted to wing commander on 1 July. The squadron, equipped with Lockheed Hudsons, primarily performed maritime patrols in the southern waters until 5 December, when four of its planes were dispatched to Darwin, Northern Territory, due to concerns about Japanese aggression in the Pacific. On 7 December, this unit set up at Penfui, near Koepang in Dutch Timor, while the remaining eight Hudsons of No. 2 Squadron were positioned in Darwin on alert. The next day, realizing Australia was now engaged in the Pacific conflict, a Hudson from Penfui attacked the suspected Japanese radio ship Nanyo Maru, causing it to run aground. By 12 December, Headlam had moved to Penfui to serve as the commanding officer of both the base and No. 2 Squadron.

In January 1942, the aircraft of No. 2 Squadron were stationed at Penfui, <unk> Island, and Darwin. The detachment at Penfui targeted Japanese ships involved in the invasion of Celebes. On January 11, two Hudsons managed to shoot down or damage three Japanese floatplanes that attacked them while they were bombing a transport ship; however, the following day, both Hudsons were downed by Mitsubishi Zeros. The first Japanese bombing of Penfui occurred on January 26, 1942, with subsequent regular attacks causing damage to some aircraft. The undamaged Hudsons were moved back to Darwin, but Headlam and his team stayed at Penfui to support reconnaissance flights from Australia. On February 18, Headlam received orders to evacuate all personnel except a small group tasked with demolishing the airfield, with help from Sparrow Force. He returned to Darwin the next day, coinciding with the city's first Japanese air raid. Four Hudsons from No. 2 Squadron were destroyed during this attack; the surviving aircraft were then moved to Daly Waters, from where they continued reconnaissance and bombing operations against Japanese targets in Timor.

Headlam stayed in Darwin as Controller of Operations at Headquarters North-Western Area Command until May 12, 1942, after which he was transferred to Nhill, Victoria, to serve as the commanding officer of No. 2 Air Navigation School, which used Ansons. In June, No. 97 (Reserve) Squadron was established using personnel from the school. On July 20, 1943, Headlam assumed command of No. 2 Air Observer School, also utilizing Ansons, located in Mount Gambier, South Australia. He was elevated to the rank of group captain on December 1, 1943, and on December 9, he became the first commanding officer of No. 3, operating both Ansons and Fairey Battles from Port Pirie. Following his tenure at No. 3, he began his studies at the RAAF Staff School in Mount Martha, Victoria, on October 2, 1944. On January 12, 1945, he was appointed as the senior administrative staff officer at North-Western Area Command.

In January 1946, Headlam was appointed as Officer Commanding North-Western Area. Later that year, he was transferred to Britain, where he attended the Royal Air Force Staff College in Andover and worked at the RAAF Overseas Headquarters in London. Upon returning to Australia in November 1947, he took up the position of Director of Training at RAAF Headquarters. In November 1950, Headlam assumed command of No. 90 (Composite) Wing from Group Captain Paddy Heffernan. Based at RAF Changi in Singapore, No. 90 Wing oversaw RAAF operations during the Malayan Emergency, including No. 1 (Bomber) Squadron, which operated Avro Lincolns, and No. 38 (Transport) Squadron, which flew Douglas C-47 Dakotas. The Lincolns carried out area bombing and targeted strikes on communist-held areas, while the Dakotas handled courier services, VIP transportation, medical evacuations across Southeast Asia, and in Malaya, they airlifted troops and supplies, dropped provisions to allied forces, and distributed propaganda leaflets. On December 20, Headlam sustained minor injuries when a No. 38 Squadron Dakota he was co-piloting crash-landed at Kampong Aur in Pahang due to engine failure during a supply mission. In August 1951, he was appointed commander of RAF Tengah in Singapore, while still holding his position as commanding officer of No. 90 Wing. He relinquished command of No. 90 Wing in December 1951.

On February 19, 1952, Headlam was appointed as the senior air staff officer (SASO) at Eastern Area Command in Penrith, New South Wales. During his tenure as SASO, the RAAF started to upgrade its fleet with English Electric Canberra jet bombers and CAC Sabre jet fighters. The Air Force also experienced a significant organizational overhaul, shifting from a geographically-oriented command-and-control structure to a function-based system, which led to the creation of Home (operational), Training, and Maintenance Commands. Due to its control over numerous combat units, Eastern Area Command was effectively an operational headquarters and was restructured into Home Command in October 1953. In recognition of his "exceptional ability and devotion to duty," Headlam was made an Officer of the Order of the British Empire (OBE) in the 1954 New Year Honours. He was promoted to acting air commodore in May and his role as aide-de-camp to Queen Elizabeth II was announced on October 7, 1954.

On January 1, 1955, Headlam was elevated to the rank of substantive air commodore. In November of that year, he was assigned to the RAAF Overseas Headquarters in London, and in the subsequent year, he pursued studies at the Imperial Defence College. Upon his return to Australia, he took on the role of acting Air Member for Personnel at the Department of Air in Canberra from March 19, 1957, to October 21, 1957, serving between the tenures of Air Vice Marshals Fred Scherger and Allan Walters, and again from August 24, 1959, to March 28, 1960, between the terms of Walters and Air Vice Marshal Bill Hely. In this capacity, Headlam was a member of the Air Board, the governing body of the service, which included its senior officers and was led by the Chief of the Air Staff. Additionally, he was one of two RAAF representatives on a committee, led by businessman William John Allison, that reviewed defense service conditions; the committee's suggestions resulted in a doubling of flight pay, among other enhancements. Headlam also held other roles at the Department of Air, including Air Commodore Plans from October 1957 to January 1959, and Director General Plans and Policy from January to August 1959. The latter position placed him in charge of the RAAF's Directorate of Intelligence. In the 1958 Queen's Birthday Honours, gazetted on June 3, Headlam was appointed a Commander of the Order of the British Empire (CBE). In May 1960, he assumed the role of acting Deputy Chief of the Air Staff.

On January 30, 1961, Headlam became part of the Operational Command (OPCOM) team, which had taken over from Home Command and was tasked with overseeing the operations of RAAF units. In April, he assumed the role of Air Officer Commanding (AOC) of OPCOM from Air Vice Marshal Val Hancock. On May 29, Headlam was elevated to the rank of air vice marshal. On July 17, 1962, he was transferred to RAAF Base Butterworth in Malaya, and a week later, he was appointed AOC of No. 224 Group RAF in Singapore. Air Vice Marshal Alister Murdoch succeeded him as AOC of OPCOM. As the head of No. 224 Group, Headlam was in charge of regional air defense and offensive air operations during the Brunei Rebellion in December 1962, and the ensuing Konfrontasi between Indonesia and Malaysia, which officially started the following month. After divorcing his first wife in 1956, he wed the widowed social worker Vernon Spence at the Sydney registry office on January 20, 1964. On November 30, he relinquished command of No. 224 Group to Air Vice Marshal Christopher Foxley-Norris.

Upon returning to Australia, Headlam was appointed Deputy Chief of the Air Staff (DCAS) on January 26, 1965. On June 22, he was honored as a Companion of the Order of the Bath (CB) for his notable service in the Borneo Territories. During his time as DCAS, the Air Force underwent its most substantial rearmament effort since World War II, amidst manpower shortages due to this expansion and Australia's growing role in Southeast Asian security. Towards the end of his term, the RAAF deployed its first helicopters to the Vietnam War. In March 1966, Headlam accompanied Lieutenant General Sir John Wilton, the Chief of the General Staff, to Saigon to strategize the deployment. The previous year, Wilton had suggested to Air Marshal Murdoch, the Chief of the Air Staff, that two Iroquois helicopters be dispatched to Vietnam for acclimatization, but Murdoch declined, leaving the RAAF helicopter squadron inadequately prepared for its army cooperation role upon deployment. On August 8, 1966, Headlam took over from Air Vice Marshal Douglas Candy as AOC Support Command in Melbourne. Support Command was established in 1959 through the consolidation of the RAAF's former Training and Maintenance Commands. On January 1, 1968, Headlam was assigned to London as the Head of the Australian Joint Services Staff. From November 17, 1970, to June 5, 1971, he served as an Extra Gentleman Usher to the Queen.

In June 1971, Headlam returned to Australia and took resettlement leave prior to his retirement from the Air Force on August 3. He settled in Melbourne, where he passed away at the age of 62 on December 23, 1976, following a long fight against cancer. He was survived by his children and second wife, and after a private funeral, he was cremated at Springvale Crematorium.

M-82 is a state highway in Michigan's Lower Peninsula, connecting Fremont to Howard City. The stretch from Newaygo to Howard City passes through Fremont and skirts the southern boundary of the Manistee National Forest. This version of M-82 is the second of its kind in Michigan; the original was established in the Upper Peninsula by 1919. The current route in the Lower Peninsula has been operational since the 1920s. Over the years, the route has seen several extensions and reductions, with its western end once reaching as far as New Era or Hesperia. The present configuration of the route was established in the late 1970s.

M @-@ 82 starts at an intersection with M @-@ 120 and B @-@ 96 west of Fremont, located at a tripoint of county boundaries. M @-@ 120 delineates the north-south boundaries between Newaygo-Oceana and Newaygo-Muskegon counties. B @-@ 96, marking the east-west boundary between Oceana and Muskegon counties, extends westward from this junction. From the intersection, M @-@ 82 heads east, traveling along 48th Street through rural farmland into Fremont. Within the town, the route becomes Main Street, traversing the downtown area before turning south onto Stewart Avenue to exit the town. The road then curves and becomes 72nd Street, heading east through additional farmland. As M @-@ 82 nears Newaygo, the landscape shifts to more wooded areas near the Muskegon River. The highway continues east on Fremont Street to meet M @-@ 37, where the two routes join and cross the river into downtown Newaygo via State Street. South of downtown, M @-@ 82 diverges eastward from M @-@ 37, following 82nd Street along the southern border of the Manistee National Forest. The eastern terminus of M @-@ 82 is at exit 118 on US 131 / M @-@ 46, west of Howard City.

The Michigan Department of Transportation (MDOT) monitors traffic volumes on its roadways as part of its maintenance duties. This is measured using the average annual daily traffic (AADT) metric, which estimates the typical daily traffic on a road segment throughout the year. In 2009, MDOT data showed that the highest traffic volume on M-82, west of Fremont, reached 16,532 vehicles per day. Conversely, the lowest traffic volume was recorded east of Newaygo, with 4,018 vehicles daily. Furthermore, no part of this highway is included in the National Highway System, which comprises roads vital to the nation's economy, defense, and mobility.

The existing M @-@ 82 was established in 1926. It extended from US 31 in Hart to the northern intersection of US 131 and M @-@ 46 in Howard City. The route passed through Ferry, Hesperia, and Fremont, taking over from M @-@ 41. By late 1936, M @-@ 46 was lengthened to include the stretch between Newaygo and Howard City, creating a concurrent route with M @-@ 82 to bridge a gap in the M @-@ 46 route. This overlapping section was designated solely as M @-@ 46 in 1938, reducing M @-@ 82's endpoint to the northern M @-@ 37 junction in Newaygo. In late 1947 or early 1948, the highway was rerouted west of Ferry. Rather than continuing northwest to Hart, it was extended westward to terminate in Shelby.

In 1963 and 1964, the western terminus of the highway was realigned once more. This adjustment shifted the route from Hesperia to New Era, circumventing Ferry. A significant alteration occurred around 1969, reshaping the highway designations within Oceana County. M-20 took over from M-82 west of Hesperia, extending to New Era rather than Muskegon. The new M-120 designation superseded M-20 south of Hesperia. Consequently, M-82 was reduced to a route solely between Hesperia and Newaygo. The highway's length was extended in 1973 when its eastern end was reestablished at Howard City. M-46 was redirected to align with the US 131 freeway south of Howard City to Cedar Springs, and it replaced M-57 between Cedar Springs and Casnovia. This adjustment allowed the segment from Newaygo to Howard City to revert to the M-82 designation. The final modification occurred in 1978, when the overlap with M-120 was discontinued in favor of extending M-120. At that point, M-82 was shortened to terminate at the junction west of Fremont, establishing the present-day configuration of the highway.

Shikamaru Nara (Nara Shikamaru) is a character from the Naruto manga and anime, crafted by Masashi Kishimoto. Within the series, Shikamaru is depicted as a ninja from the Konohagakure village. He is part of Team 10, alongside Choji Akimichi, Ino Yamanaka, and their leader Asuma Sarutobi. Known for his laziness, Shikamaru possesses exceptional intelligence but is often reluctant to use it; Kishimoto appreciates Shikamaru's laid-back personality. Beyond the Naruto manga and anime, Shikamaru appears in four of the series' movies, and in various other media such as video games and original video animations.

Various anime and manga sources have discussed Shikamaru's personality. Critics often highlight his laziness alongside his intelligence, and observe his evolution into a leadership role; Anime News Network praised Shikamaru's rise as "an unexpected hero" within the Naruto narrative. Shikamaru enjoys significant popularity among Naruto fans, consistently ranking well in numerous popularity surveys. Merchandise featuring Shikamaru, such as action figures, keychains, and patches, has also been made available.

Masashi Kishimoto has expressed his fondness for Shikamaru, appreciating his laid-back demeanor despite his genius, and he juxtaposed this with Sasuke Uchiha's smart yet harsh character. Kishimoto humorously stated that he would marry Shikamaru if he were female, pointing out Shikamaru's potential for success in life. For Shikamaru's design in Part II, Kishimoto aimed to craft a distinctive look for him, even though he outfitted him with a vest common among other ninja in the series. To ensure his hair remained visible, he placed Shikamaru's forehead protector on his arm.

Shikamaru's initial significant role in the series occurs during the Chunin Exams, which are held every two years for ninjas aspiring to elevate their rank. He is a member of Team 10, together with Choji Akimichi and Ino Yamanaka. Known for his lack of enthusiasm, Shikamaru strives to navigate life with the least amount of effort possible. Despite his apparent laziness, he possesses exceptional intelligence; his mentor, Asuma Sarutobi, assessed Shikamaru's IQ to be above 200. Shikamaru's skills revolve around the Shadow Imitation Technique (Kage Mane no Jutsu, known on English TV as "Shadow Possession Jutsu"), a hallmark ability of his clan that allows him to fuse his shadow with that of an adversary, rendering them immobile and compelled to replicate Shikamaru's actions. As the narrative advances, Shikamaru develops new methods to control his shadow. By the second part of the series, he can employ several shadow-based techniques simultaneously and can elevate his shadow off the ground to engage with tangible objects, such as impaling foes with shadow tendrils or hurling weapons using them.

Shikamaru faces the exams with indifference; during his fight against Temari from Sunagakure, he emerges victorious but concedes the match to her because of his depleted chakra. Despite this defeat, he is the sole ninja in his group to advance to Chunin rank, as the exam supervisors were impressed by his strategic thinking and intelligence displayed in the battle with Temari. As a Chunin, Shikamaru is tasked with leading a team to stop Sasuke Uchiha from defecting to Otogakure. Although his team successfully overcomes the Otogakure ninja obstructing them, Sasuke still manages to flee.

In the second installment of the series, Shikamaru is tasked with tracking down two members of the nefarious Akatsuki group. Although his team successfully locates their targets, the immortal Akatsuki member Hidan slays Asuma Sarutobi in battle, despite Shikamaru's utmost efforts to prevent it. Following Asuma's funeral, Shikamaru, along with the remaining members of Team 10 and with assistance from Kakashi Hatake, embarks on a mission to avenge their fallen mentor. While the others confront Hidan's partner Kakuzu, Shikamaru exacts revenge on Hidan, ensuring that the Akatsuki member's body is never recovered. After the confrontation, Shikamaru pledges to safeguard Kurenai Yuhi and Asuma's newborn child. Subsequently, he is assigned to the Fourth Division with Temari and Choji, serving as a deputy general under Gaara. In the series' epilogue, expressing his personal aspirations during the final conflicts, Shikamaru ascends to the role of advisor to the Seventh Hokage, Naruto, after marrying Temari and fathering a son, Shikadai Nara.

In addition to the Naruto anime and manga, Shikamaru appears in seven films within the series. In the second film, he assists Naruto Uzumaki and Sakura Haruno in their battle against Haido, a utopian idealist aiming to dominate the world using a power known as <unk>. In the fourth film, Shikamaru is seen briefly fighting a large group of stone soldiers. The fifth film sees Shikamaru, along with Kakashi and Sai, searching for the Land of Sky's base, which intends to attack Konoha. In the sixth film, Shikamaru, Sakura, and Sai confront a chimera beast summoned by Hiruko. In the eighth film, he battles the demon Satori. The ninth film introduces a portly Shikamaru in the Limited Tsukuyomi universe, contrasting sharply with his teammate <unk>, who takes on the role of team strategist. In the tenth film, Shikamaru leads a team including himself, Naruto, Sakura, Sai, and Hinata Hyuga on a mission to rescue Hinata's younger sister, Hanabi, who was abducted by <unk> Otsutsuki. Additionally, Shikamaru features in the third original video animation, participating in a tournament. He is a playable character in almost all Naruto video games, such as the Clash of Ninja and Ultimate Ninja series. Some games feature unique variations of his Shadow Imitation Technique not shown in the anime or manga. Naruto Shippūden: Gekitō Ninja Taisen! EX 2 is the first game to showcase Shikamaru's Part II appearance.

A light novel called Shikamaru Hiden: A Cloud Drifting in Silent Darkness, authored by Takashi Yano and illustrated by Kishimoto, features Shikamaru as both the protagonist and narrator. Set two years following the Fourth Ninja War, the story centers on Shikamaru's role as the coordinator of the newly established Shinobi Union, tasked with apprehending a renegade ninja who governs the remote Land of Silence and seeks to create a new world order led by the masses. The narrative also delves into his developing relationship with Temari, which eventually leads to his difficulty in choosing a name for their child, long after the novel concludes.

Shikamaru consistently ranks well in the Weekly Shōnen Jump popularity polls for the series, often securing a spot in the top ten and once achieving fourth place. The most recent poll, conducted in 2011, saw him ranked ninth, surpassing Hinata but trailing Sasori. Various Shikamaru-themed merchandise has been produced, such as action figures, key chains, and patches reflecting his looks from both Part I and Part II. NTT subscribers ranked him as their sixteenth favorite anime character with black hair. Hiroshi Matsuyama, the CEO of CyberConnect2, has cited Shikamaru as one of his top characters from Naruto.

Numerous sources covering manga, anime, video games, and related media have discussed Shikamaru's character. Meridian ranks as the sixth largest city in Mississippi, USA. It serves as the county seat for Lauderdale County and is the main city within the Meridian, Mississippi Micropolitan Statistical Area. Positioned along key highways, Meridian lies 93 miles (150 km) east of Jackson, Mississippi; 154 miles (248 km) west of Birmingham, Alabama; 202 miles (325 km) northeast of New Orleans, Louisiana; and 231 miles (372 km) southeast of Memphis, Tennessee.

Founded in 1860 at the junction of the Mobile and Ohio Railroad and the Southern Railway of Mississippi, Meridian's economy thrived on the railroads and the commodities they carried, establishing it as a key trading hub. In the American Civil War, during the Battle of Meridian in February 1864, General William Tecumseh Sherman razed much of the city to the ground.

Following its reconstruction post-war, the city experienced a "Golden Age," becoming Mississippi's largest city from 1890 to 1930 and a key manufacturing hub in the South, serviced by 44 daily trains. Union Station, constructed in 1906, has evolved into a multi-modal facility, connecting users to the Meridian Transit System, Greyhound Buses, and Trailways, with an annual passenger throughput of 242,360. Despite economic challenges following the downturn of the railroad sector, the city has broadened its economic base, with healthcare, military, and manufacturing sectors being the top employers in 2010. The city's population was estimated at 38,232 in 2008, but within a 45-mile (72 km) radius, it expands to 232,900, and within a 65-mile (105 km) radius, it reaches 526,500. Of these, 104,600 and 234,200 individuals, respectively, are part of the workforce, contributing to the city's economy.

The region is supported by two military installations, Naval Air Station Meridian and Key Field, which together offer more than 4,000 jobs. NAS Meridian hosts the Regional Counter-Drug Training Academy and the state's first local Department of Homeland Security. Key Field honors the Key brothers, Fred and Al, who achieved a world endurance flight record in 1935. Currently, it houses the 186th Air Refueling Wing of the Air National Guard and serves as a support facility for the 185th Aviation Brigade of the Army National Guard. In the area, Rush Foundation Hospital stands as the largest non-military employer, with a workforce of 2,610 individuals.

Among the numerous arts organizations and historic structures in the city are the Riley Center, the Meridian Museum of Art, the Meridian Little Theatre, and the Meridian Symphony Orchestra. Meridian housed two Carnegie libraries, segregated into one for whites and another for African Americans. The Carnegie Branch Library, which has since been demolished, was among several Carnegie libraries constructed for African Americans in the Southern United States during the time of segregation.

The city has been chosen as the site for the upcoming Mississippi Arts and Entertainment Center (MAEC). Jimmie Rodgers, known as the "Father of Country Music," was born in Meridian. A museum in Highland Park showcases artifacts from his life and career, along with steam-engine era railroad equipment. The park also features the Highland Park Dentzel Carousel, recognized as a National Historic Landmark and the only existing two-row stationary Dentzel menagerie worldwide. Other prominent figures from Meridian include Susan Akin, Miss America 1986, James Chaney, a civil rights activist murdered during the 1964 Mississippi civil rights workers' killings, and Hartley Peavey, who founded Peavey Electronics, based in Meridian. The federal courthouse in the city hosted the 1966-1967 trial of those accused in the murder of Chaney and two other activists, marking the first instance where a white jury convicted a white official for a civil rights-related killing.

The region, once home to the Choctaw Native Americans, was acquired by the United States through the Treaty of Dancing Rabbit Creek in 1830, during the Indian Removal era. Following the treaty's ratification, European-American settlers started to relocate to the area now known as Meridian.

Upon receiving a federal land grant of approximately 2,000 acres (810 ha), Richard McLemore, the initial settler of Meridian, started providing free land to new arrivals to entice further settlement and foster growth in the area. In 1853, the majority of McLemore's land was purchased by Lewis A. Ragsdale, an attorney from Alabama. The remaining 80 acres (0.32 km2) were acquired by John T. Ball, a merchant from Kemper County. Recognized as the city's founders, Ragsdale and Ball proceeded to plan and allocate plots for new developments on their respective properties.

There was significant contention regarding the naming of the settlement. Ball and the city's more industrial inhabitants favored "Meridian," equating it with "junction"; in contrast, the more rural residents preferred "<unk>" (translating to "mad river" in a Native American tongue), derived from a local creek's name; meanwhile, Ragsdale suggested "Ragsdale City." Ball constructed a station on the Mobile and Ohio Railroad, with its sign switching between "Meridian" and "<unk>" daily. Ultimately, the expansion of the railroads brought in numerous railroad workers who outvoted the others, resulting in "Meridian" being fixed on the station. The town was formally established as Meridian on February 10, 1860.

At the onset of the American Civil War in 1861, Meridian was a modest village. Due to its critical location at a railroad junction, the Confederates built numerous military facilities to aid their efforts. In the 1864 Battle of Meridian, General William Tecumseh Sherman commanded his troops into the town, demolishing the railroads in all directions, along with an arsenal and vast warehouses; his troops razed many structures to the ground. Sherman reportedly remarked afterward, "Meridian, with its depots, storehouses, arsenal, hospitals, offices, hotels, and barracks, no longer exists." Despite the devastation, the city's railroad tracks were quickly restored, resuming service just 26 days after the battle. During the Reconstruction period, racial tensions persisted, culminating in the 1871 riot sparked by a fire that harmed numerous businesses.

Following the Civil War, the town thrived and entered its "Golden Age" from 1880 to 1910. The local railroads facilitated transportation and attracted various industries, leading to a surge in population. With the growing population, commercial activities in the downtown area flourished. From 1890 to 1930, Meridian became the biggest city in Mississippi and a key manufacturing hub in the South. During and shortly after this period, many of the city's historic structures were constructed, such as the Grand Opera House in 1890, the Wechsler School in 1894, two Carnegie libraries in 1913, and the <unk> Building, Meridian's tallest skyscraper, completed in 1929.

The city's expansion persisted due to the commission government's initiative to introduce 90 new industrial facilities in 1913 and the flourishing automobile sector in the 1920s. Despite the 1929 stock market crash and the subsequent Great Depression, the city remained appealing to new enterprises. As escapism gained traction in the culture during the worst of the Depression, the S. H. Kress & Co. building, designed to "offer luxury to the common man," was established in downtown Meridian, along with the Temple Theater, which served as a cinema. The federal courthouse, constructed in 1933, was a project of the WPA.

Following a short economic downturn at the conclusion of the Depression, the nation engaged in World War II, revitalizing the significance of railroads. These railways were crucial for moving gasoline and scrap metal needed for military vehicle production, thus reestablishing Meridian as the regional rail hub. This resurgence of prosperity lasted until the 1950s, when the rise in popularity of automobiles and the Interstate Highway System overshadowed passenger rail services. The subsequent decline of the railroad sector led to substantial job cuts, prompting a decrease in population as employees migrated to other regions.

In the 1960s, during the American Civil Rights Movement, Meridian housed an office for the Council of Federated Organizations (COFO) and various other activist groups. Local residents like James Chaney, along with northern volunteers Michael Schwerner, his wife Rita, and Andrew Goodman, endeavored to establish a community center. They conducted classes to empower African Americans in the region to reclaim their voting rights. The activism provoked resentment among local whites, frequently leading to violent racial conflicts. In June 1964, Chaney, Schwerner, and Goodman traveled to Neshoba County, Mississippi, to connect with members of a black church that had been attacked and set ablaze. That night, the trio vanished while returning to Meridian. After an extensive FBI investigation, their bodies were discovered two months later, buried in an earthen dam.

Seven members of the Ku Klux Klan, including a deputy sheriff, were found guilty in the Meridian federal courthouse of "violating the victims' civil rights," while three were cleared in the trial concerning the murders of civil rights workers in Mississippi. This marked the first instance where a white jury convicted "a white official for a civil rights murder." In 2005, the state reopened the case and filed charges for the first time. Edgar Ray Killen was convicted of manslaughter and received a 60-year prison sentence. Subsequently, Meridian paid tribute to Chaney by renaming a section of 49th Avenue in his honor and conducting an annual memorial service.

From the 1960s onward, with the development of highways facilitating easier travel, people started relocating from the city center to new residential areas in the north. As commercial strip developments began encroaching on downtown areas, the city took action in the 1970s and 1980s to establish multiple historic districts to maintain the city's architectural integrity. In 1979, the Meridian Historic Districts and Landmarks Commission was established, followed by the founding of the Meridian Main Street program in 1985.

Meridian Main Street spearheaded multiple initiatives to rejuvenate the downtown area, such as building a new Amtrak Station in 1997, modeled after the historic train station from Meridian's Golden Age that had previously been torn down. Additional efforts included the restoration of the Rosenbaum Building in 2001 and Weidmann's Restaurant in 2002, alongside promoting cohesive urban planning. In collaboration with The Riley Foundation, Meridian Main Street also facilitated the renovation and transformation of the historic Grand Opera House in 2006 into the "Mississippi State University Riley Center for Education and the Performing Arts."

Following the transfer of Meridian Main Street's ownership to the Alliance for Downtown Meridian in late 2007, the Alliance, together with the Meridian Downtown Association, led the initiative for downtown revitalization. The Alliance functions as a central organization, providing its support staff and facilities to the other two groups, and acts as a coordinator among them. There were plans to refurbish the <unk> Building, but these were canceled by the newly elected Mayor Cheri Barry in early 2010. Currently, the Alliance works to encourage additional development and restoration in the downtown area, aiming to support businesses like specialty stores, restaurants, and bars, which contribute to increased activity both day and night. The Meridian Downtown Association concentrates mainly on boosting pedestrian traffic downtown through the organization of special events, while the Meridian Main Street program aids existing downtown businesses.

Due to Meridian's role as a railroad hub, the influx of travelers has spurred the establishment of numerous hotels. Prior to Meridian's "Golden Age," several significant hotels such as the Great Southern and the Grand Avenue were erected before the 20th century began. As the railroad network expanded and the original Union Station was completed in 1906, a surge in hotel construction catered to both passengers and railroad employees. The Elmira Hotel was built in 1905, followed by the Terminal Hotel in 1910. Hotel Meridian was constructed in 1907, and the Union Hotel in 1908. In 1979, the Union Hotel was added to the National Register of Historic Places, while Hotel Meridian and the Grand Avenue Hotel were recognized as contributing elements to the Meridian Urban Center Historic District.

As the city expanded, the hotels mirrored the robust economic aspirations, exemplified by the eleven-story Lamar Hotel skyscraper constructed in 1927. In 1979, it was added to the National Register of Historic Places and converted into a county annex building. By 1988, it had been designated as a Mississippi Landmark.

Constructed in 1931, the E.F. Young Hotel became a key establishment in the African-American commercial area that emerged west of the city's center. During the era of segregation, it stood out as one of the few locations in the city where a traveling African American could secure lodging.

During the 1960s and 1970s, as suburban areas of the city expanded, the majority of hotels relocated away from the downtown area. The revitalization of the Riley Center in 2006 spurred increased interest and a demand for a new hotel in the downtown district. The <unk> Building was suggested for redevelopment to meet this need, but the project was hindered by a shift in city leadership. In response, the <unk> Preservation Society was established in 2013 to boost public awareness and garner support for the building's restoration, organizing first-floor tours and celebratory events to mark anniversaries.

Meridian features nine historic districts recognized on the National Register of Historic Places. The Meridian Downtown Historic District merges two previously established districts: the Meridian Urban Center Historic District and the Union Station Historic District. These areas showcase a variety of architectural styles, predominantly from the late 19th and early 20th centuries, such as Queen Anne, Colonial Revival, Italianate, Art Deco, Late Victorian, and Bungalow. Since 1985, Meridian has been governed by the mayor-council or "strong mayor" system. Every four years, the mayor is elected by the entire populace. The city council, consisting of five members, is also elected every four years, with each member representing one of the city's five wards, which are designated as single-member districts. As the city's chief executive officer, the mayor oversees and directs the daily operations of the municipal government. The city council serves as the legislative branch, responsible for establishing policies and approving the city's annual operating budget.

City Hall, registered on the National Register of Historic Places, is situated at 601 23rd Avenue. The mayor currently serving is Percy Bland. The city council consists of Dr. George M. Thomas representing Ward 1, Kenneth Dustin Markham from Ward 2, Barbara Henson from Ward 3, Kim Houston from Ward 4, and Randy Hammon from Ward 5. Pam McInnis serves as the council clerk. The city has a total of 570 employees.

Shortly after Hurricane Katrina in 2005, the city set up a Department of Homeland Security (DHS), marking it as the only local DHS within the state. This department manages a region spanning nine counties. After securing $2.5 million in grants from the Mississippi Emergency Management Agency and various other groups, the DHS started training law enforcement personnel from other Southern states in passenger rail rescue operations and also began providing civilian courses in basic handgun use, Boy Scout first aid and hunting, and firearms training. During emergencies like Hurricane Ivan in September 2005, the DHS played a crucial role by setting up and maintaining shelters for 700 evacuees. Currently, the city leads one of the task forces in the Mississippi DHS, which consists of three teams each covering nine counties.

Since 2009, the Meridian Police Department, led by Chief Lee <unk>, has comprised 115 full-time officers along with part-time and reserve personnel. That year, the department's Criminal Investigations Division handled 4000 cases, half of which were felonies. In 2000, the number of reported crimes was <unk>, a slight increase from the 2008 crimes reported the previous year. Meridian is often referred to as "the safest city in Mississippi with a population over 30,000." The East Mississippi Correctional Facility, situated in unincorporated Lauderdale County near Meridian, is managed by the GEO Group for the Mississippi Department of Corrections. Anthony Clayton serves as the chief of the Meridian Fire Department, which in 2009 responded to over 1600 calls, including 123 structural fires and 609 emergency service calls.

In state politics, the city is segmented into three sections by the Mississippi Senate district map. The northernmost part of the city falls within the 31st State Senate District, represented by Terry Clark Burton (R). A section stretching from the southwest to the northeast of the city is included in the 32nd State Senate District, represented by Sampson Jackson, II (D). The western and southeastern areas of the city are part of the 33rd State Senate District, represented by <unk> Carmichael (R). The central area of the city constitutes all of House District 82, represented by Wilbert L. Jones (D). House District 83, which encircles District 82, is represented by Greg Snowden (R).
