At the national level, Meridian is situated in Mississippi's 3rd congressional district, which is represented by Gregg Harper (R), who has held the position since 2009. Since 1972, Lauderdale County, where Meridian is located, has consistently voted for the Republican presidential candidate. Before this shift towards the Republican Party, the white voters in the area backed Democratic candidates, as the state had been dominated by a single party, the Democrats, since the late nineteenth century.

The city's development has been influenced by various social and economic forces. From its establishment until 1970, the population grew in every census, with growth rates ranging from a high of 165% to a low of 0.2%. The population saw a decline in the 1970 census, a minor rise by 1980, followed by a gradual decrease, and then an increase since the beginning of the 21st century. From 1980 to 2000, there was a population drop of over 14%. According to the 2000 census, the city had a population of 39,968 with a population density of 885.9 people per square mile (342.0/km2). In 2008, it ranked as the sixth largest city in the state. The population saw an increase by 2010.

Meridian serves as the main city within the Meridian metropolitan region, encompassing three counties—Clarke, Kemper, and Lauderdale—as of 2009, with a total population of 106,139. Within a 45-mile (72 km) radius, the population reaches 232,900, and within a 65-mile (105 km) radius, it extends to 526,500.

Although the city's total population growth has fluctuated, there has been a consistent increase in both the number and proportion of non-white residents. The sole decrease in this demographic occurred between 1960 and 1970, coinciding with a significant drop in the city's overall population. According to the 2010 Census, the city's racial composition was 61.55% African American, 35.71% White, 0.9% Asian, 0.2% Native American, less than 0.02% Pacific Islander, 0.59% from other races, and 0.89% from two or more races. Individuals of Hispanic or Latino origin, regardless of race, constituted 1.75% of the population.

According to the 2000 Census, out of the 17,890 housing units within the city boundaries, 15,966 were occupied, with 10,033 of these being family households. Of the occupied households, 31.1% included children under 18 years old, 36.2% were married couples cohabiting, 23.3% were headed by a female without a husband, and 37.2% were non-family households. Additionally, 33.2% of all households consisted of individuals living alone, and 14.0% of these were individuals aged 65 or older living by themselves. The average household size was 2.39, while the average family size was 3.06. Since 1970, when the average household size was 3.04, it has been steadily declining. The median age in Meridian rose from 30.4 in 1970 to 34.6 by the year 2000.

The median household income in the city was $25,085, while the median family income was $31,062. The median income for males stood at $29,404, compared to $19,702 for females. The city's per capita income was $15,255. Approximately 24.6% of families and 28.6% of the population lived below the poverty line, which included 40.8% of individuals under 18 years old and 22.0% of those aged 65 and above.

The community in Meridian and its vicinity is notably religious, with 65.2% of Lauderdale County residents identifying as members of a religious group, which is higher than the national average of 50.2%. In 2000, among those affiliated, 30,068 individuals (59.0%) belonged to the Southern Baptist Convention, 9,469 (18.6%) were part of the United Methodist Church, and 1,872 (3.7%) were connected to the Catholic Church.

Jews who migrated from Germany and eastern Europe played a significant role in the city's commercial growth, establishing various businesses and services. Congregation Beth Israel was established in 1868, right before the onset of the city's "Golden Age." At one point, Meridian boasted the state's largest Jewish community, with a population of 575 Jews in 1927. Currently, the number of Jews residing in Meridian has dwindled to less than 40, predominantly elderly individuals.

Meridian is situated in Lauderdale County within the North Central Hills region of Mississippi. As per the United States Census Bureau, the city encompasses a total area of 45.9 square miles (119 km2), with 45.1 square miles (117 km2) being land and 0.8 square miles (2.1 km2) being water. Positioned along major highways, Meridian lies 93 miles (150 km) east of Jackson, Mississippi; 154 miles (248 km) west of Birmingham, Alabama; 202 miles (325 km) northeast of New Orleans, Louisiana; 231 miles (372 km) southeast of Memphis, Tennessee; and 297 miles (478 km) west of Atlanta, Georgia. The landscape around the city features cotton and corn fields, as well as oak and pine forests, and is characterized by clay hills and the low-lying areas at the headwaters of the <unk> River.

The urban center of the city has altered the natural landscape through grading, yet the surrounding regions retain their gently undulating nature. The city is crisscrossed with numerous small streams, and features small lakes and forested areas in its northern and southern sectors. <unk> Creek flows through the southern part of the city and splits into Gallagher's Creek, which traverses the city's center. Loper's Creek winds through the city's far-western section, while smaller streams such as Shearer's Branch, Magnolia Creek, and Robbins Creek are scattered across the city.

Meridian falls within the humid subtropical climate zone. During the summer months of June to August, the average high temperature is approximately 90°F (32°C), while the average low is about 70°F (21°C). In the winter, spanning December to February, the average high temperature is around 60°F (16°C) and the average low is about 35°F (2°C). July is the warmest month, with an average high of 92.9°F (33.8°C), whereas January is the coldest month, with an average low of 34.7°F (1.5°C).

The city experiences an average yearly precipitation of 58.65 inches (1,490 mm). Rainfall is spread quite uniformly across the year, with March being the wettest month, receiving an average of 6.93 inches (176 mm) of rain. A significant portion of the rainfall comes from thunderstorms, which are frequent in the summer but happen year-round. Occasionally, severe thunderstorms occur, bringing not only lightning and heavy rain but also potentially destructive winds and large hail. These severe storms are most frequent in spring, with another increase in frequency during the fall, and they also pose a risk of tornadoes.

Initially, the economy was heavily reliant on the local railroads. At the beginning of the 20th century, the city was the biggest in Mississippi, serviced by five major rail lines and seeing 44 trains daily. The economy thrived not just on the railroads themselves but also on the commodities like timber and cotton that they transported. Thanks to these rail-dependent industries, the city emerged as a significant economic force in the state and region from approximately 1890 to 1930. However, as the railroad industry declined in the 1950s, the city's economy also slowed. In response, the city transitioned from an economy predominantly based on railroads to a more varied one, with key sectors now including healthcare, military, and manufacturing.

Meridian, along with Lauderdale County and the city of Marion, is supported by the East Mississippi Business Development Corporation, established in 1996 by local business leaders. As of April 2010, the city had a civilian labor force of just 15,420, yet within a 45-mile (72 km) radius, the population reaches 232,900, and within a 65-mile (105 km) radius, it extends to 526,500, with labor forces of 104,600 and 234,200 respectively. Consequently, Meridian acts as a central point for employment, retail, healthcare, and cultural activities. Eighty percent of the workforce in Lauderdale County lives within the county, and ninety percent reside within a 45-mile radius.

In April 2010, Lauderdale County had 6,260 individuals working in the healthcare sector. The biggest healthcare employer in the area is Rush Hospital, with 2,610 employees, followed by East Mississippi State Hospital with 1,500, and Anderson Hospital with 1,475 staff members. Meridian hosts three hospitals along with numerous other healthcare-related establishments. Jeff Anderson Regional Medical Center offers cardiovascular surgery, a Level II newborn intensive care unit, and a health and fitness center. Rush Foundation Hospital and its associated Rush Health Systems manage the Specialty Hospital of Meridian, providing long-term care for patients needing extended recovery time in a hospital environment. Riley Hospital operates two facilities focused on stroke treatment and rehabilitation. Additional healthcare facilities in Meridian include the Alliance Health Center and East Mississippi State Hospital, the latter having been operational since 1882.

Retail is a significant source of employment in the county, with 5,280 individuals working in the sector as of April 2010. Annually, the city sees nearly $2 billion in retail spending. The Bonita Lakes Mall, spanning 633,685 square feet (58,871 m2), hosts over a hundred shopping options, ranging from department stores and specialty shops to restaurants, dining spots, and United Artists Theatres. The first phase of Meridian Crossroads, a 375,000-square-foot (34,800 m2) shopping complex in the Bonita Lakes vicinity, was finalized in November 2007, significantly enhancing the local retail landscape. Additionally, the North Hills Street shopping area has seen ongoing expansion, and in March 2007, new retail and office spaces were introduced near the Highway 19 Walmart Supercenter.

The region is supported by two military installations, Naval Air Station Meridian and Key Field, which together provide more than 4,000 jobs to the local community. NAS Meridian is dedicated to training naval carrier pilots and other enlisted members. It also hosts the Regional Counter-Drug Training Academy (RCDATA), offering narcotics training to law enforcement across numerous southeastern states. The city, which hosts the state's first local Department of Homeland Security, leads a nine-county regional response team and a twenty-nine-county regional response task force. Key Field gained fame from the historic flight of brothers Fred and Al Key, who achieved a world endurance flight record in 1935. Currently, Key Field serves as the base for the 186th Air Refueling Wing of the Air National Guard and a support facility for the 185th Aviation Brigade of the Army National Guard. Additionally, it features an aviation history exhibit and houses Meridian's Aviation Museum.

In April 2010, Lauderdale County had a total of 2,850 individuals employed in manufacturing. Peavey Electronics Corporation, known for producing guitars, amplifiers, and sound equipment since 1965, is headquartered in the city. Additional companies operating in the region include Avery Dennison, Structural Steel Services, Sara Lee, Tower Automotive, and <unk> Corporation. The city also hosts four industrial parks.

In the downtown area, the MSU Riley Center generates income through tourism, arts, and entertainment. Annually, it draws over 60,000 visitors to downtown Meridian for various conferences, meetings, and shows. On Front Street, Loeb's Department Store stands as a historic clothing landmark in Mississippi, having been managed by four generations of the same family. Since its inception by Alex Loeb in 1887, the store has been offering high-quality clothing for men and women.

Meridian, renowned for over a century of artistic heritage, is home to numerous art and cultural organizations and hosts a variety of cultural events. The Meridian Art League, one of the earliest art organizations in the city, was founded in February 1933. Initially, art exhibitions took place at the Lamar Hotel in downtown Meridian. Following a renaming to the Meridian Art Association in 1949, the exhibitions began to occur at different venues throughout the city. After the Carnegie library at 25th Ave and 7th St shut down, the Art Association transformed the building into the Meridian Museum of Art, establishing a permanent venue for exhibitions. The museum opened its doors in 1970 and has since offered rotating exhibitions alongside numerous educational programs for both students and adults. Annually, over thirty exhibitions are showcased, covering a spectrum from traditional decorative arts to ethnographic and tribal materials, photography, crafts, and various other art forms. The museum's collection also features 18th and 19th-century portraits, 20th-century photography, and several sculptures.

The Meridian Council for the Arts (MCA) was established in 1978 as the official arts agency for Meridian and Lauderdale County. Each year, MCA runs its Community Art Grants program, the annual <unk> Festival, various workshops, and other special events. MCA collaborates with numerous arts organizations within the city and county, such as the Meridian Museum of Art, the Meridian Little Theatre, and the Meridian Symphony Orchestra. The Meridian Little Theatre, one of the oldest subscription-based community theatres in the South, was constructed in 1932 and now entertains over 22,000 guests each season, making it the most attended community theatre in Mississippi for residents and visitors of Meridian and Lauderdale County. The Meridian Symphony Orchestra (MSO), founded in 1961, held its first concert in 1962 and its first complete season in 1963. In 1965, the MSO engaged its first international soloist, Elena <unk>, to perform. The Orchestra has supported the Meridian Public School District in developing its own orchestra and strings programs and has also contributed to the development of the Meridian Symphony Chorus. Dr. Claire Fox Hillard, the current conductor, has been with the orchestra since 1991. The MSO is set to celebrate its 50th anniversary in February 2011 with a performance by Itzhak Perlman.

The former Grand Opera House in the city was constructed in 1889 by half-brothers Israel Marks and Levi Rothenberg. Throughout its run, it featured numerous renowned artists and productions, debuting with a German company's performance of Johann Strauss II's "The Gypsy Baron." The opera house shut down in the late 1920s due to the Great Depression and remained deserted for almost 70 years. In 2000, a $10 million grant from the Riley Foundation, established locally in 1998, initiated the restoration of the building, supplemented by $15 million from municipal, county, and national grants. The renovation concluded in September 2006, and the venue was rechristened as the "Mississippi State University Riley Center for Education and Performing Arts." The Riley Center now features a 950-seat auditorium for live shows, a 200-seat studio theater, and 30,000 square feet (2,787 square meters) of space for meetings, drawing over 60,000 visitors to downtown Meridian each year for various events and performances.

Meridian is rightfully regarded as an architectural gem, being one of the most preserved cities from the early 20th century in the country. It attracts groups of architecture students from across the U.S. and Canada who come to study the numerous buildings designed by renowned architects. The only house in the southern U.S. designed by the celebrated Canadian-born architect Louis S. Curtiss, known for his invention of the glass curtain wall skyscraper, still stands in Highland Park. The <unk> Building, designed by Frank Fort, is widely regarded as one of the finest Art Deco skyscrapers in the U.S. and is frequently likened to Detroit's iconic Fisher Building. Noted California architect Wallace Neff also contributed to Meridian's architectural landscape, designing several homes there and in the adjacent Alabama Black Belt. Neff, who had family members in Meridian and Selma working as railroad industry executives, took on projects in the region during slower periods in California. His designs are primarily found in the lower-numbered blocks of Poplar Springs Drive, where his <unk> Poplar Springs Drive is often compared to Falcon Lair, the Benedict Canyon home of Rudolph Valentino in Beverly Hills. Unfortunately, one of Neff's works was demolished during an expansion of Anderson Hospital in 1990, and another was destroyed by fire in Marion Park during the 1950s. Additionally, the Meridian Post Office, with its interior completely clad in bronze and Verde marble, stands out as an excellent example of the type of post office buildings constructed in prosperous cities during the 1920s. It originally featured <unk> lighting, which was regrettably removed during a 1960s renovation and is now found in private homes on Poplar Springs Drive and in North Hills.

Meridian has been chosen as the site for the forthcoming Mississippi Arts and Entertainment Center (MAEC). The Mississippi Legislature endorsed the project in 2001 and committed $4 million in 2006, contingent on private donors raising $8 million. In September 2007, the city contributed $50,000 to the project. The proposed MAEC will occupy 175 acres (71 ha) at Bonita Lakes, featuring an outdoor amphitheater, an indoor concert hall, and a Hall of Fame dedicated to Mississippi artists. Early public education in Meridian was established under the 1870 Mississippi Constitution. Between 1870 and 1885, the City Council appointed trustees to the Board of School Directors, which was responsible for managing the schools. Prior to 1884, the city had several schools, but these were privately operated and served only around 400 students. The first publicly owned school in the city was not constructed until September 1884. The initial public school for African Americans was conducted in spaces leased from St. Paul Methodist Church. In January 1888, the Mississippi Legislature modified the city's charter to permit the establishment of a municipal school district, and in March of that year, the city approved $30,000 in bonds to fund the construction of new public schools. Using funds from this bond, the Wechsler School was erected in 1894, marking it as the first brick public school building in the state designated for African Americans.

The Meridian Public School District expanded from its initial area and subsequent expansions to its present scale, now comprising six elementary schools, three middle schools, and three high schools. It caters to students in grades 10-12 and has an enrollment of around 1,500 students.

Harris Junior College in 1970, which had exclusively served African-American students. The institution's name was updated from Meridian Junior College to Meridian Community College in 1987 "to better represent the varied opportunities it offers to an expanding community." Papa Stour, part of Scotland's Shetland Islands, has a population of fewer than twenty, including some who moved there following a 1970s call for new residents. Situated west of Shetland's mainland, the island covers 828 hectares (3.2 square miles), making it the eighth largest in the Shetland group. The erosion of its soft volcanic rock by the sea has formed a remarkable range of caves, stacks, arches, blowholes, and cliffs. The island and its waters are home to a variety of wildlife. The western part of Papa Stour is designated as a Site of Special Scientific Interest, and the surrounding marine areas are classified as a Special Area of Conservation.

The island features multiple Neolithic burial chamber locations and the ruins of Duke Hakon's house from the 13th century, during the Norse settlement. In the 19th century, the population peaked at 380 or higher following the establishment of a fishing station at <unk> in West Voe. Since then, the population has steadily decreased, though it has risen from a minimum of 16 in the 1970s.

Papa Stour lies at the southwestern tip of St Magnus Bay. It features 34 kilometers (21 miles) of rugged coastline, marked by many small inlets and four larger 'voes'. Housa Voe, meaning 'harbour bay' in Old Norse, is situated in the south and offers the most sheltered anchorage, with its surrounding cliffs featuring a natural rock arch. In contrast, Hamna Voe, or 'house bay' in Old Norse, located to the east, is less secluded but serves as the island's primary harbor and the point where the ferry departs.

Holm and Maiden Stack stand sentinel at the southern entrance to the harbor. Holm, a tidal island, served as a leper colony until the 18th century, though it's speculated that many of the so-called "lepers" actually suffered from a vitamin deficiency rather than leprosy. Maiden Stack's name stems from a 14th-century tale in which Lord Thorvald constructed a small house at its summit to "protect" his daughter from suitors. The ruins of this house remain visible today. However, his plan failed when his daughter left and was discovered to be pregnant; an alternative version of the story tells of her successful elopement with a fisherman. On the north coast, West Voe, with its inner section known as 'Clousta Voe,' is the primary inlet, with the smaller Burra Voe located directly to the west.

The primary settlement on the island now is <unk>, situated with a view over <unk> Voe and encircled by in @-@ bye land east of the hill dyke (extending south from West Voe). A strip of glacial moraine, approximately one and a half kilometers long, divides the island to the west. The remainder of the island features a thin, rocky soil possibly originating from glacial till. Peat is nearly nonexistent on the island, and thanks to the volcanic rocks, the soil remains quite fertile. The scarcity of peat resulted in 'turf scalping' for fuel, leaving exposed rock surfaces in the island's interior.

On June 21, 2008, Stuart Hill, the sole owner and resident of the 1-hectare (2.5-acre) island known as <unk> Holm, which he renamed "<unk> Island," issued a declaration of dependence, establishing the Crown Dependency of <unk>. The island consists of various volcanic and sedimentary rock types from the Devonian era. During this time, the Scottish landmass was a component of the Old Red Sandstone Continent, positioned approximately 10 to 25 degrees south of the equator. The deposits of Old Red Sandstone, which formed between 408 and 370 million years ago, resulted from the erosion of earlier Silurian rocks uplifted during the creation of Pangaea, and were subsequently deposited in river deltas. The freshwater Lake Orcadie bordered the eroding mountains, extending from Shetland to the southern Moray Firth. The composition of Papa Stour predominantly features ashes and lavas from volcanic activity during this period, including layers of solidified volcanic ash and lava (rhyolite), alongside a Devonian fish bed located at Lamba Banks. Additionally, numerous large boulders were left by Pleistocene glaciation.

The sea's erosion of the soft volcanic rocks has formed an impressive array of caves, stacks, arches, blowholes, cliffs, voes, and other features, which rank among the best in Britain. The 'Holl o' cave extends completely through the north-west tip of the island, stretching nearly half a mile and wide enough for rowing. In the south-west, 'Christie's Hole' is another remarkable cave, where part of the roof caved in during 1981. Additionally, 'Francie's Hole' near Voe in the west was a favorite of John Tudor, who documented the island in his Victorian memoirs and praised the cave's allure.

Otters, grey seals, killer whales, and harbour porpoises are commonly observed on and around Papa Stour. Species such as the Atlantic puffin, Arctic and common tern, <unk> and Arctic skua, northern fulmar, common guillemot, razorbill, curlew, wheatear, ringed plover, and great black-backed gull breed on the island, with many migratory birds also documented there.

A variety of wildflowers, such as mountain everlasting, spring squill, and <unk>, along with the widespread heather, abound. The island's human habitation began around 3000 BC, with evidence of multiple Neolithic burial sites called 'heel-shaped cairns'. Details about the pre-Celtic and Celtic periods are scarce, but upon the Norse's arrival, they probably encountered a religious community. The island's name, which comes from a term meaning "Big island of the Papar" (referring to Celtic monks), distinguishes it from Papa Little, located about 12 kilometers (7.5 miles) to the west.

A manuscript from 1299, written in Old Norse and the oldest surviving document from Shetland, focuses on Papa Stour. It recounts a dramatic event at the residence of Duke Hakon Magnusson, who eventually became King Hakon V of Norway. In 1469, Shetland came under the nominal control of Scotland, yet the Norse 'Lairds of Norway' retained their estates on Papa Stour until the 17th century. During the 16th century, merchants from Bremen and Hamburg ran a summer trading post to purchase fish from the local fleet. By the 18th century, the island was owned by two Scottish lairds, Thomas Gifford of Busta and Arthur Nicolson of Lerwick. They supported a thriving deep-sea fishing industry, known in Old Norse as 'haff', which operated during the summer using six-oared boats called 'færing'.

During the 19th century, the <unk> fishing station in West Voe began operations, and the island's population reached at least 360 residents. Yet, from the 1870s, the population declined due to fuel shortages and reduced fishing activity following the advent of steam drifters. Concurrently, another notable event marked Papa Stour's history. Notable instances of horizontal water mills, referred to as Norse or Clack Mills, can be found near Dutch Loch. These mills were traditionally two-story structures with turf roofs, integrated into slopes to facilitate entry to the upper level where the millstone was located. Within the structure, a stationary lower millstone and a rotating upper millstone, powered by water cascading onto the paddles beneath, were housed. Some of these mills remained operational in Papa Stour into the early 20th century, and a functional example still exists on the Burn of <unk> at <unk> in the southern part of Shetland's Mainland.

Like many small Scottish islands, Papa Stour's population reached its highest point in the 19th century and has since seen a considerable decrease (see, for example, Mingulay). By 1970, the island's school had shut down, and the number of residents had dwindled to sixteen 'fairly elderly' individuals. However, an advertisement in Exchange and Mart turned the tide. It offered a croft and five sheep at no cost to newcomers, resulting in a surge of applicants. The 1981 census showed a population increase to 33. Yet, by 2005, the population had dropped to 20 following severe disputes among residents, which led to multiple court cases. Several people moved away, and the school closed again. The Aberdeen trawler Ben Doran, wrecked on the Ve Skerries 3 miles northwest of Papa Stour, on the evening of March 28, 1930, while en route to Scalloway village to offload its catch. Although the weather was relatively calm when it ran aground, it wasn't until the next day that another trawler noticed and reported the incident. By the time rescue operations were initiated by the coastguard and local volunteers (with no lifeboat available in Shetland at the time), the weather had worsened, making it impossible to reach the skerries. A call for the Stromness lifeboat from Orkney, just 120 miles away, was made, but it was too late to provide assistance. All 9 crew members perished in the disaster. Only three bodies were found: James Mitchell, whose body was sent back to Aberdeen, and J. Cormack and J.R., whose bodies were interred in Scalloway.

In February 1940, the cargo vessel SS Highcliffe ran aground on <unk> Holm due to foggy conditions. Fortunately, the weather was mild, and only the ship and its cargo were lost. In 1967, the Aberdeen trawler Juniper grounded in Lyra Sound at the base of cliffs measuring 60 meters (200 feet). All 12 crew members were saved by the <unk> lifeboat, and the coxswain received the RNLI silver medal for his bravery during the rescue.

The most recent shipwreck at Papa Stour happened on December 9, 1977, when the Aberdeen trawler Elinor Viking, under the command of skipper Alec Flett, ran aground on the Ve Skerries. Although the lifeboat arrived at the site, it couldn't approach closely enough to save the crew due to rough seas. Following a call from Alec Webster, the Coastguard Station Officer in Lerwick, a volunteer team from Sumburgh Airport piloting a British Airways Sikorsky helicopter was dispatched. Despite fierce storm winds, they successfully airlifted all crew members to safety shortly after the vessel grounded. The helicopter team was later honored with several bravery awards. While no lives were lost, this event led to the construction of a lighthouse on the skerries in 1979 and might have been the catalyst for establishing the current Search and Rescue helicopter unit at Sumburgh Airport.

"Angel of Death" serves as the lead song on the 1986 album Reign in Blood by the American thrash metal group Slayer. The song's lyrics and composition were crafted by the band's guitarist, Jeff Hanneman, inspired by the notorious Nazi doctor Josef Mengele, who performed horrific experiments on humans at the Auschwitz camp during World War II. The track "Angel of Death" resulted in ongoing allegations of Nazi sympathies and racism against the band throughout their career.

Despite the disputes over the song and its role in postponing the release of Reign in Blood, "Angel of Death" is included in all of Slayer's live albums and DVDs, and it has been showcased in various films. The track was praised by reviewers; Steve Huey from AllMusic referred to it as a "classic".

Jeff Hanneman, the guitarist from Slayer, penned "Angel of Death" inspired by literature on Nazi doctor Josef Mengele he encountered during a tour. He recalled, "I stopped somewhere and picked up two books on Mengele. I thought, 'This must be really twisted.' When we started working on the album, those ideas were still fresh in my mind—that's where the lyrics for 'Angel of Death' originated."

The song's lyrics describe the horrific surgical experiments conducted by Mengele on victims at the Auschwitz concentration camp during World War II. His studies targeted groups like dwarfs and twins, involving both physical and psychological assessments. The specific experiments highlighted in "Angel of Death" include surgeries done without anesthesia, blood transfusions between twins, tests on isolation endurance, gassing, injections with deadly bacteria, sex reassignment surgeries, as well as the removal of organs and limbs, and other unspecified procedures.

"Coming together, merging minds. It's only a matter of time before you tear yourselves apart," a lyric from the second-to-last verse, alludes to the accusation that Mengele surgically connected twins, with one being deformed; "the hunchback was attached to the other child, back to back, their wrists also joined in the same manner." This accusation was initially brought to light by Auschwitz survivor Vera Alexander during the 1961 trial of SS officer Adolf Eichmann, known as the "architect of the Holocaust," where it was claimed that Mengele "joined their veins" and transformed "them into conjoined twins." The allegation gained broader recognition when Vera Alexander appeared in the 1985 documentary The Search for Mengele, which has been referenced by numerous authors, including Mengele expert Gerald Posner.

The lyrics of "Angel of Death" were a factor in delaying the release of Slayer's album Reign in Blood in 1986. Slayer was under contract with Def Jam Records, but their distributor, Columbia Records, declined to distribute the album because of its lyrics and cover art, which they considered "too graphic." Ultimately, Geffen Records took over the distribution of Reign in Blood, releasing it on October 7, 1986. Despite this, due to the surrounding controversy, the album was not included in Geffen Records' official release schedule.
